newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan government grows more confident of recovery.
newsitem.headline: Japan government grows more confident of recovery.

text.p: Japan's government expressed growing confidence in the nation's economic recovery on Friday, saying a recent sales tax rise would not hurt the economy much.

Growing optimism over the economy, meanwhile, prompted a sharp drop in Japanese government cash bonds and futures as speculation grew that the Bank of Japan might tighten interest rates as early as July.
Economic Planning Agency (EPA) Minister Taro Aso told reporters that the fall-off in consumer spending in reaction to the sales tax rise would not be that great.
"The impact has been within expectations," he said, adding that the economy was continuing its gradual recovery and was on an upward trend.
Japan lifted its sales tax to five percent from three percent on April 1 as part of government measures to clamp down on spending and increase revenues.

A consumer rush to buy luxury goods and make savings on the larger purchases in life such as cars ahead of the tax increase had prompted fears that the resulting drop in spending after the rise would take the wind out of the recovery.
But an EPA survey released Thursday showed that many retail outlets, including department stores and car dealerships, expect consumer spending to recover from July.

Akira Furukawa, the director of the EPA's national economic research bureau, also said that while the agency needed to keep its eyes on the impact of the sales tax increase, better employment conditions and firm wage growth would support consumption.
"The economy as a whole is entering a favourable economic cycle," he told Reuters Financial Television.
While some economists said they agreed with the government, others were more cautious.

Yoshikazu Shimada, an economist at Kankaku Research Institute, said that while he agreed the fall in consumer spending would slow over the next few months, consumer purchasing power would remain weak overall.
"Wages in real terms are going to fall and affect consumption. As such I don't think we can expect much vigour in the recovery," he said.
But most economists dismissed speculation of a rate rise out of hand.
"I don't buy the rate hike story at all," said Ron Bevacqua, an economist at Merrill Lynch Japan. "There is no inflation pressure and all these other pressures against it."

Bevacqua said it was still too early for a rate rise, given government fiscal tightening measures, problems still plaguing the banking sector, land prices still not having bottomed out and U.S. pressure to increase domestic demand.
